summary:
Earth Jukebox is an interactive web experience that transforms NASA Earth Information Center imagery into original, dynamically generated soundscapes. Users explore a 3D globe, select regional night-light studies, and discover a library of NASA visualizations covering oceans, aerosols, air quality, carbon dioxide, lightning, atmospheric rivers, and forests.

The application maps visual features including brightness, color, and spatial distribution to musical parameters such as pitch, note strength, rhythm, and stereo position. Users can isolate individual voices and compare India’s and Ukraine’s 2012 and 2023 night-light images using a shared audio scale. Each study includes source credits and an explanation of its sound mapping and limitations.

Earth Jukebox addresses the challenge by pairing NASA visuals with sound that responds directly to their image content. It offers an engaging, multisensory way to explore Earth science, supporting curiosity and learning through both sight and hearing. Its sonifications interpret rendered imagery rather than claiming to reproduce environmental recordings or calibrated measurements.
details:
Earth Jukebox is an interactive web experience that lets people explore NASA imagery through sight and sound. Our goal is to make Earth science more engaging by turning patterns in visualizations into original soundscapes that users can explore, compare, and understand.

What it does and how it works

Users enter through a revolving 3D Earth and explore regional night-light studies or a library of NASA visualizations. The library covers ocean currents and temperature, aerosols, air quality, carbon dioxide, lightning, atmospheric rivers, and forest height. We also include NASA’s Caldwell 73 astronomy visualization as a separate educational reference.

The application analyzes visual features such as brightness, color, edges, and spatial distribution. It maps these features to musical properties, including pitch, note strength, rhythm, and stereo position. Different subjects use distinct sound designs so that exploring an ocean visualization feels different from exploring lightning or atmospheric particles.

Audio is synthesized directly in the browser rather than selected from prerecorded music. Users can play and pause, adjust volume, move through the image scan, and isolate individual musical voices. An audio-reactive waveform makes the generated sound visible.

For India and Ukraine, users can compare night-light imagery from 2012 and 2023. Both years use a shared calibration, helping listeners explore visual differences under consistent audio mapping. Each study provides source attribution and an explanation of its interpretation and limitations.

Benefits and intended impact

Earth science imagery can contain patterns that are difficult to notice at first glance. Sonification offers another way to explore those patterns: bright clusters, contrasting colors, and spatial changes become audible variations.

We designed Earth Jukebox for curious learners, educators, and public audiences. Its intended impact is to encourage exploration of NASA resources and spark conversations about our changing planet. Combining visual exploration with sound creates an additional route into scientific content.

Keyboard controls, descriptive text, and reduced-motion support help broaden access. However, we have not validated the experience with blind or low-vision participants, so we do not claim it replaces accessible scientific descriptions.

Tools and technologies

We developed the application using:

  • React and TypeScript for the interface and application logic.
  • Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei for the interactive globe.
  • Tone.js and the Web Audio API for browser-based sound synthesis.
  • HTML Canvas for image analysis and audio visualization.
  • Python scripts for preparing imagery and extracting source frames.
  • Vite for development and production builds.
  • Vitest and Playwright for automated logic and browser testing.
  • GitHub for version control and Vercel for hosting.

The experience runs in a modern browser without dedicated hardware. Headphones help listeners distinguish stereo positioning and individual voices. Prepared NASA assets are served with the application; this version does not fetch live observations.

We used AI assistance for coding, interface development, debugging, and testing. The soundscapes themselves are generated by explicit image-analysis and synthesis rules, not a generative AI music model.

What makes it creative

Earth Jukebox treats the planet as an interface and sound as a way to investigate imagery. Rather than placing background music behind NASA visuals, it makes the visual content drive the audio.

Our creative challenge was balancing interpretability with musicality. Topic-specific instruments and musical rules make the output approachable, while voice isolation and mapping explanations let users investigate how it was produced. The paired night-light studies extend this idea into a comparative listening experience.

Factors we considered

We prioritized scientific honesty, source attribution, responsive design, performance, and clear audio controls. We also preserved the distinction between global visualizations and geographically bounded regional studies.

Our sonifications interpret rendered imagery, not calibrated measurements of temperature, radiance, pollution, or carbon dioxide. The playback scan represents movement across an image, not the passage of observation time. Regional crops can include neighboring territory, and audible differences alone cannot establish the causes of environmental change.

These boundaries are central to our approach: Earth Jukebox invites people to explore NASA imagery through a new sensory experience while remaining transparent about what the sounds represent.
